519.title: Nitzavim: you can return (Deuteronomy 30:1–3)
519.hook: however far scattered, a person and a people can return
519.howItsDone: Teshuvah, returning, is the central theme of the Hebrew month of Elul and the High Holy Days; Deuteronomy 30 is read in synagogue in the weeks just before Rosh Hashanah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a covenant with those not here this day. Your line was those not yet here. What did you do for someone in the future? Today, a promise for people who drift far. Day five hundred nineteen.

After you've drifted from something, there comes a moment when the distance itself starts to feel like the reason you can't go back. You haven't called a friend in two years, so now it's too awkward to call. You stopped a practice, and starting again feels like admitting you ever stopped. The gap becomes the wall. Deuteronomy thirty is written for people standing on the far side of that gap. And it says, again and again, that the gap is not a wall.
screen: `TWO YEARS WITHOUT A CALL.` → `THE GAP BECOMES THE WALL.` → `THE GAP IS NOT A WALL.`

segments.voice: The chapter imagines the worst. The blessings and the curses have all come true, and the people are scattered among the nations. Then, it says, when you take it to heart there, wherever there is, and return to God and listen with all your heart and all your soul, God will return to you and gather you in. Even, verse four adds, if you've been driven to the far edge of the heavens. The Hebrew root running through these verses is shuv: turn, turn back, return. It comes again and again in a few lines. People return, God returns, the scattered are brought back. From the same root comes teshuvah, usually translated repentance, but closer to returning. It fits that this portion is read in the season just before Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, the days most focused on teshuvah. Notice what the text doesn't say. It doesn't say: if you never wander. It assumes the wandering. It sets no distance beyond which return stops working. And notice the order. The people turn first, and then God turns too. A step from one side is met by a step from the other. The medieval teacher Nachmanides reads the verses right after this, about a commandment that isn't too hard or too far away, as being about teshuvah itself. Return, he says, is within reach.
screen: `SCATTERED AMONG THE NATIONS.` · `SHUV: TURN, TURN BACK, RETURN.` · `NO DISTANCE TOO FAR.` · `ONE STEP MET BY ANOTHER.` · then, large: `YOU CAN RETURN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take one step back toward something good. Settle, and breathe. Think of something good you've drifted from. A person, a habit, a place, a practice, a part of yourself. Notice the gap, and notice any voice saying it's been too long. Now don't plan the whole road back. Just pick the first step. One message. One page. One walk. One short visit. Picture yourself taking it, and picture it being met. The bell holds the time.
Nitzavim. Standing. And in it, shuv: the turning back that the chapter says is always possible.
Your line: you can return. Today, take the first small step back toward one good thing you've drifted from. Day five hundred nineteen.

520.title: Nitzavim: very nigh (Deuteronomy 30:11–14)
520.hook: the word is not in heaven or across the sea, "the word is very nigh unto thee"
520.howItsDone: 'It is not in heaven' (lo bashamayim hi) is one of the best-known principles of rabbinic law: Jewish law is decided by sages through study and majority, as told in the Talmud's story of the oven of Akhnai.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shuv, the turning back. Your line was you can return. Did you take a first step toward something? Today, how far away it really is. Day five hundred twenty.

When something matters, we tend to put it far away. Real wisdom must live on a mountaintop, or in a book you'll never finish, or with a teacher in another country. Real change must need a retreat, a new city, a fresh start in January. The distance protects us a little. If it's far, nobody can blame us for not reaching it. Moses takes that excuse apart in four verses.
screen: `ON A MOUNTAINTOP, IN ANOTHER COUNTRY.` → `A FRESH START IN JANUARY.` → `THE EXCUSE OF DISTANCE.`

segments.voice: "For this commandment which I command thee this day, it is not too hard for thee, neither is it far off. It is not in heaven." No one needs to climb up and fetch it. Nor, Moses goes on, is it beyond the sea, so that someone has to sail across and bring it back. "But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it." In thy mouth: you can say it. In thy heart: you can understand it. That thou mayest do it: you can live it. The Hebrew for near is karov, the same word for a close relative. This verse has a famous second life in the Talmud. In Bava Metzia, the rabbis argue about whether a certain kind of oven can become ritually impure. Rabbi Eliezer is outvoted, and calls on miracles to prove he's right. A carob tree uproots itself. A stream flows backward. Finally a voice from heaven says the law is with Eliezer. Rabbi Joshua stands up and quotes our verse: it is not in heaven. The Torah has already been given; now it's decided here, by people, by the majority. The story ends with a report that God smiled and said, My children have defeated Me. Two readings of one phrase. Deuteronomy says: the Torah isn't out of reach. The Talmud adds: and once it's in your hands, it's yours to work out.
screen: `NOT IN HEAVEN.` · `NOT BEYOND THE SEA.` · `IN THY MOUTH, IN THY HEART.` · `RABBI JOSHUA AND THE OVEN.` · then, large: `VERY NEAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do the good thing close at hand. Settle, and breathe. Let your attention come in close: your breath, your hands, the room you're in. Now ask, what good thing is within arm's reach today? Not the big plan. The near one. A call you could make in five minutes. A kind word to someone in your house. A dish to wash, a bill to pay, an apology you already know the words to. Find it, and let it sit right there, close. The bell holds the time.
Nitzavim. Standing. And karov: near, very near, in your mouth and in your heart.
Your line: very near. Today, skip the faraway plan once, and do the good thing that's right in front of you. Day five hundred twenty.

521.title: Nitzavim: choose life (Deuteronomy 30:19)
521.hook: "I have set before thee life and death... therefore choose life"
521.howItsDone: 'Choose life' is among the most quoted verses in Jewish teaching on ethics and free will, and the everyday toast l'chaim, 'to life', is heard at nearly every Jewish celebration.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the word that's very near, in your mouth and in your heart. Your line was very near. What good thing did you find close at hand? Today, the last lines of Nitzavim, and a choice. Day five hundred twenty-one.

At Jewish celebrations, sooner or later someone lifts a glass and says l'chaim. To life. It's said over wine at a wedding, over whiskey at a bris, over a paper cup at a retirement party. It's so ordinary that hardly anyone stops to wonder why that's the toast. Not to luck, not to health, not to money. To life. Today's verse puts that same word, chayim, life, at the center of the Torah's last great choice.
screen: `A GLASS LIFTED.` → `L'CHAIM: TO LIFE.` → `THE SAME WORD IN THE TORAH.`

segments.voice: Moses is near the end of his speech. He calls heaven and earth to witness and says: "I have set before thee life and death, the blessing and the curse; therefore choose life, that thou mayest live, thou and thy seed." Notice the odd extra step. If someone offered you life or death, you wouldn't need advice about which to pick. So why say it? Rashi imagines a father with his son. He stands the boy in front of the best plot of his land and says: choose this one for yourself. The advice isn't there because the answer is hard to see. It's love, pointing. Another reading hears the verse as a statement that the choice is real. Maimonides, the twelfth-century philosopher and legal scholar, drew on this chapter in his teaching on free will. A person isn't fated to be good or bad. Each person can choose. And the verses right after say what life means here: to love God, to listen, to hold fast. Life, in this verse, is more than breathing. It's a way of living that leads to more life. Then the last words: thou and thy seed. Your choice reaches your children. Choosing life is rarely one big moment. It's thousands of small ones: a glass lifted, a meal shared, a hard thing faced instead of avoided, a day lived toward something good.
screen: `LIFE AND DEATH, SET BEFORE YOU.` · `RASHI: A FATHER POINTING.` · `MAIMONIDES: THE CHOICE IS REAL.` · `THOUSANDS OF SMALL CHOICES.` · then, large: `CHOOSE LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make one life-giving choice. Settle, and breathe. Think about the rest of today. Somewhere in it there's a fork, maybe a small one. Eat something real or skip it. Go outside or stay in. Call someone or keep scrolling. Rest, or push through when you shouldn't. Name the fork. Then picture taking the side that gives a little more life, to you or to someone else. Feel what that choice is like in your body before you make it. The bell holds the time.
Nitzavim. Standing. And the choice set before everyone standing there: life.
Your line: choose life. Today, at one small fork, take the side that gives a little more life. And if you lift a glass tonight, you'll know the toast. Day five hundred twenty-one.

522.title: Vayelech: Moses went (Deuteronomy 31:1)
522.hook: at the end, Moses goes out to the people rather than calling them in
522.tomorrow: Vayelech: strong and of good courage (Deuteronomy 31:7)
522.howItsDone: Vayelech is read in the fall, near Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, and is often paired with Nitzavim; teachers frequently draw from its opening the value of a leader going out to the people.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the great choice: life and death, the blessing and the curse. Your line was choose life. Which fork did you take? Today, a new portion, the shortest in the Torah, and its first two words. Day five hundred twenty-two.

When an important person wants to speak with you, you usually go to them. You're called into the office. You wait outside a door. You're given a time slot. Leaders summon; that's part of what power looks like. At the very end of his life, Moses has more authority than anyone in the camp. He could have every tribe brought before his tent. And the portion opens with him doing the opposite.
screen: `CALLED INTO THE OFFICE.` → `LEADERS SUMMON.` → `MOSES DOES THE OPPOSITE.`

segments.voice: "And Moses went and spoke these words unto all Israel." In Hebrew, vayelech Moshe: and Moses went. Readers have always asked, went where? He wasn't on a journey. The text doesn't say. So the commentators fill the silence, each a little differently. Ibn Ezra suggests he went from tribe to tribe through the whole camp, to tell each one in person that he was about to die, and to strengthen them. Nachmanides pictures him going out to the people the way someone about to leave goes to say goodbye to a friend, as a mark of respect. Either way, the man who spoke with God doesn't call the people in for one final address. He walks to them. In the very next verse he tells them why it's now: "I am a hundred and twenty years old this day; I can no more go out and come in." He's reached his limit. And before it closes, he spends what strength is left going out one more time. The portion named for this moment, Vayelech, is the shortest in the Torah, only thirty verses. Maybe that fits. A last visit doesn't need to be long. It needs to happen. A leaving can be done by announcement, by a notice on the wall. Moses chooses to do it in person, tent by tent.
screen: `VAYELECH: AND HE WENT.` · `WHERE? THE TEXT IS SILENT.` · `TRIBE BY TRIBE, TO SAY GOODBYE.` · `A HUNDRED AND TWENTY, STILL GOING.` · then, large: `HE WENT TO THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go to someone yourself. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you've been waiting to hear from. A friend who's gone quiet, a relative you only see when they visit you, a neighbor you'd talk to if only they knocked. Notice the waiting. Now picture reversing it. You walk to their door, or pick up the phone, or send the first message. Not a summons; a visit. See their face when it's you who came. The bell holds the time.
Vayelech. And he went. The first word of the shortest portion in the Torah.
Your line: he went to them. Today, instead of waiting for someone to come to you, go to them: a visit, a call, a first message. Day five hundred twenty-two.

screen: `DAY 522 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: VAYELECH: STRONG AND OF GOOD COURAGE (DEUTERONOMY 31:7).`

523.title: Vayelech: strong and of good courage (Deuteronomy 31:7)
523.hook: Moses encourages Joshua in front of all Israel
523.howItsDone: When the reading of each of the five books of the Torah is completed in synagogue, the congregation calls out 'chazak, chazak, venitchazek', be strong, be strong, and let us be strengthened.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vayelech: Moses went out to the people. Your line was he went to them. Who did you go to? Today, what he says to the man who will take his place. Day five hundred twenty-three.

Most encouragement happens in private. A text before an interview. A hand on the shoulder in a hallway. A quiet good luck at the door. Private encouragement is real, and good. But there's another kind that's harder to give: saying it out loud, in front of everyone, so the person hears it and so does everyone around them. It costs the speaker something. It puts their own name behind someone else. Moses chooses that kind.
screen: `A TEXT BEFORE THE INTERVIEW.` → `A HAND ON THE SHOULDER.` → `OR: OUT LOUD, IN FRONT OF EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: "And Moses called unto Joshua, and said unto him in the sight of all Israel: 'Be strong and of good courage.'" In Hebrew, chazak ve'ematz. Two words that overlap: be strong, be firm. Moses had already said the same words to the whole people a few verses earlier. Now he says them to one man, in front of everyone. Think about Joshua's position. He's following Moses, the one who spoke with God face to face. Anyone in his place would wonder whether he could measure up, and whether the people would follow. A public blessing answers both doubts at once. Joshua hears that his teacher believes in him. And the people hear it too, so they know their new leader didn't grab the role. It was handed to him, with confidence, in daylight. The words keep traveling. Later in this chapter God says them to Joshua directly, and again, more than once, at the opening of the book of Joshua. And they've entered Jewish life in another form. When a congregation finishes reading one of the five books of the Torah, everyone calls out: chazak, chazak, venitchazek. Be strong, be strong, and let us be strengthened. When Deuteronomy ends, in two weeks on our path, it will be said again. Courage, in this verse, isn't something Joshua has to find alone. It's given to him, out loud, by someone who has watched him for forty years.
screen: `IN THE SIGHT OF ALL ISRAEL.` · `CHAZAK VE'EMATZ.` · `TWO DOUBTS ANSWERED AT ONCE.` · `CHAZAK, CHAZAK, VENITCHAZEK.` · then, large: `STRONG AND OF GOOD COURAGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: encourage someone publicly. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone stepping into something new or hard. A colleague in a new role, a kid trying out for something, a friend starting over. What do you honestly believe about them? Find one true sentence. Now picture saying it where others can hear it: in a meeting, at the dinner table, in the group chat. Not flattery. Just the true thing, out loud, with your name behind it. The bell holds the time.
Vayelech. And he went. And in it, chazak ve'ematz: be strong and of good courage, said in front of everyone.
Your line: strong and of good courage. Today, encourage one person where others can hear it. Day five hundred twenty-three.

524.title: Vayelech: everyone gathers (Deuteronomy 31:10–13)
524.hook: every seven years men, women, children and strangers gather to hear the Torah
524.howItsDone: Hakhel was held at the Temple during Sukkot after each sabbatical year. Since the Temple's destruction it is not performed as commanded, but some communities and organizations in Israel and elsewhere hold commemorative public readings or gatherings in that year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses encouraging Joshua in front of everyone. Your line was strong and of good courage. Who did you encourage out loud? Today, a gathering that happens once every seven years. Day five hundred twenty-four.

Stadiums fill for games. Squares fill for marches and concerts. Almost nobody fills a stadium to hear someone read aloud. Yet the Torah asks for exactly that crowd: no band, no scoreboard, just one voice, a scroll, and thousands of people standing still to listen. Men and women, toddlers on shoulders, foreigners who live in the land, all packed into one courtyard to hear words most of them already know. That is the crowd Moses commands in Vayelech, once every seven years.
screen: `A STADIUM-SIZED CROWD.` → `HERE TO HEAR A READING.` → `ONCE EVERY SEVEN YEARS.`

segments.voice: The command: at the end of every seventh year, the year of release, during the festival of Sukkot, the Torah is to be read before all Israel. "Assemble the people, the men and the women and the little ones, and thy stranger that is within thy gates, that they may hear, and that they may learn." The word for assemble gives the ceremony its name: hakhel. Gather. The Mishnah, in Sotah, says the king himself read from Deuteronomy, on a wooden platform built in the Temple courtyard. It tells a striking story. King Agrippa received the scroll standing, though he was allowed to sit. When he reached the verse forbidding a foreigner as king, he wept, because his family came from outside. And the people called out to him: don't be afraid, you are our brother. The Talmud asks a sharp question about the guest list. The men come to learn, the women come to hear. But why bring the little ones? They won't understand a word. The answer: to give reward to those who bring them. There's a plainer point in it too: a child who stands in that crowd once may remember the crowd, even without the words. Hakhel says learning isn't only private study. Sometimes everyone needs to stand in one place, the king and the toddler and the stranger, and hear the same words together. Since the Temple's destruction the ceremony hasn't been held in its old form, though some communities mark the year with gatherings of their own.
screen: `ONCE IN SEVEN YEARS, AT SUKKOT.` · `HAKHEL: GATHER EVERYONE.` · `AGRIPPA WEEPS: YOU ARE OUR BROTHER.` · `WHY BRING THE LITTLE ONES?` · then, large: `EVERYONE GATHERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: gather people to learn. Settle, and breathe. Think of a few people you could gather, even two or three. Family at dinner, friends on a call, coworkers at lunch. What's one thing worth learning together? A short text, a story from a grandparent, a recipe, a question none of you can answer alone. Picture everyone in one place, including someone who usually gets left out of these things. Then pick a day. The bell holds the time.
Hakhel. Gather. The seven-yearly assembly where everyone, from king to child to stranger, hears the Torah together.
Your line: everyone gathers. Today, invite at least one other person to learn something with you, even for ten minutes. Day five hundred twenty-four.

525.title: Vayelech: write this song (Deuteronomy 31:19)
525.hook: the Torah's last command is to write it; the Talmud says each Jew should write a scroll (Sanhedrin 21b)
525.howItsDone: A Torah scroll is written by hand by a trained scribe (sofer) on parchment; many communities celebrate the completion of a new scroll by letting members fill in its final letters, guided by the scribe.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hakhel: everyone gathering once in seven years. Your line was everyone gathers. Who did you invite to learn? Today, the last commandment, and it involves a pen. Day five hundred twenty-five.

When did you last write something out by hand that you didn't have to? Not a signature, not a shopping list. Just copying words because they mattered. A pen slows you down, and slowing down changes what you notice. You can't skim with a pen. Every letter gets a moment. Almost at its end, the Torah gives a commandment about writing. By the traditional count, it's the last commandment in the whole Torah.
screen: `NOT A SIGNATURE, NOT A LIST.` → `YOU CAN'T SKIM WITH A PEN.` → `THE LAST COMMANDMENT.`

segments.voice: God tells Moses: "Now therefore write ye this song for you, and teach thou it the children of Israel." Plainly, the song is the poem that comes next, Ha'azinu, which we'll begin in two days. But the rabbis read the verse more widely. The song, they said, means the whole Torah. And write ye means every person. In the Talmud, in Sanhedrin, the teacher Rabbah says: even if your parents left you a Torah scroll, it's a commandment to write one of your own. Maimonides counts this among the six hundred thirteen commandments, and in the Torah's order it comes last. Writing a full scroll by hand takes a trained scribe, a sofer, many months of work. So how does an ordinary person do it? Some commission a scribe. In many communities, when a new scroll is nearly finished, people each take a turn completing a letter, with the scribe guiding the hand. And some authorities, like the medieval sage known as the Rosh, taught that in later times writing or acquiring books of Torah study carries the same spirit. Underneath is a striking idea. Inheriting isn't enough. The tradition wants each person to make it their own, letter by letter. This week we walked from Nitzavim into Vayelech. You can return. Very near. Choose life. He went to them. Strong and of good courage. Everyone gathers. And now: write your own.
screen: `WRITE YE THIS SONG.` · `RABBAH: WRITE YOUR OWN SCROLL.` · `THE LAST OF THE 613.` · `ONE LETTER, GUIDED BY THE SCRIBE.` · then, large: `WRITE YOUR OWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: copy out one verse by hand. If you can, find a pen and paper. If not, trace the letters with a finger on your palm or on the table. Choose a line that's stayed with you this month. Maybe choose life, or the word is very nigh unto thee. Copy it slowly, one letter at a time. Notice where your hand hesitates. Notice a word you'd never really looked at before. The bell holds the time.
Vayelech. And he went. And in it, the last commandment: write this song. Write your own.
Your line: write your own. Today, copy one line that matters to you by hand, and keep it somewhere you'll see it. Day five hundred twenty-five.

sources.ref: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Tefillin, Mezuzah and Torah Scroll 7:1
